answer.ideal:
(a) Captain Brown asks the question. He means the farmers or other people of Concord. The British visitors have come to find out where supplies are hidden and how well the town is defended.

(b) Mr Bliss says the people will fight the British to the death. Brown swears and stamps his foot, bringing his heel down on Tabby’s hand.

(c) Supplies such as gunpowder, axes and guns are hidden in houses. The cannons are hidden in the woods. A guard of ten men patrols Concord at night.

questions.explanation: The three parts ask for the speaker and purpose of the visit, Brown’s actions after Bliss’s reply, and Concord’s hiding places and night patrol. Accept accurate equivalent wording rather than exact textbook phrases.
questions.hint: Recall who is speaking, what Brown does next, and where Concord keeps its supplies and cannons.
questions.prompt:
Read this extract from “Tabby’s Tablecloth” and answer all three parts.

“These people won’t fight, will they?”

(a) Who asks this question? Who are “these people”, and why have the visitors come to Concord? [3]

(b) What does Mr Bliss say will happen if the British attack? What does Captain Brown do next? [3]

(c) Where had the townspeople hidden their supplies and cannons? How did they watch the town at night? [3]

points.concept: Part (a): Captain Brown asks the question.
Part (a): ‘These people’ means Concord's farmers or townspeople. Saying ‘farmers in Concord’ fully covers this point.
Part (a): The visitors have come to learn where Concord’s supplies are hidden and/or how well the town is defended, so the British can attack or seize them.
Part (b): Mr Bliss says the people of Concord will fight the British to the death or resist fiercely.
Part (b): Captain Brown swears or responds angrily.
Part (b): Captain Brown stamps his foot, bringing his heel down on Tabby’s hand.
Part (c): Gunpowder, axes, guns or other supplies are hidden in houses in Concord.
Part (c): The cannons are hidden in the woods.
Part (c): A guard patrols the town at night; the exact number ten is optional.

answer.ideal:
(a) Tabby knows the two visitors are British soldiers and Mr Bliss is a Tory. She suspects they are making plans that could harm Concord, so she wants to hear their conversation.

(b) She jumps through the open window, hides under the dining table and makes herself small beneath the long tablecloth so the men cannot see her.

(c) Captain Brown stamps his foot and his heel lands on Tabby’s hand. The pain nearly makes her cry out, but she bites her lips and stays still so the men do not discover her.

questions.explanation: Tabby’s suspicion comes from the visitors being British soldiers and Mr Bliss being a Tory. answer.ideal:
(a) Mr Bliss speaks to Captain Brown and the other, junior British officer.

(b) After the men leave, Tabby escapes through the window and tells the people of Concord what she heard. The British officers are already well on their way to Boston, so they escape.

(c) Her warning gives the people time to move valuable supplies to nearby towns and get their cannons ready. They are not taken by surprise when the British attack.

questions.explanation: The extract identifies Mr Bliss and the two British officers. After they leave, Tabby escapes and warns Concord; the officers are already heading to Boston. The warning lets the town move supplies, ready cannons and avoid surprise.

answer.ideal:
(a) After the fighting, the government took over Mr Bliss’s property and sold many of his belongings at an auction. Tabby’s uncle bought the tablecloth there.

(b) Her uncle said the cloth belonged to Tabby because her quick eyes and ears had warned Concord, so the town was not taken by surprise. Tabby’s daughter later preserved it as a token of her mother’s bravery.

(c) The long tablecloth hid Tabby while she listened beneath Mr Bliss’s table. In 1861 it was made into lint and soft squares, which were used to cover or dress soldiers’ wounds.

questions.explanation: The questions follow the cloth from the auction to Tabby’s family, then ask for its two uses. Score the stated events and accept equivalent descriptions of bandages or dressings for the wounded soldiers.
